--- title: "Building an Agentic AI for VM-22 Valuation: Let the Model Orchestrate, Not Calculate" description: "How I built an AI agent that runs a principle-based reserve valuation for non-variable annuities, cites the Valuation Manual and drafts VM-31 and stakeholder reports, without ever letting the language model compute a reserve." date: "2026-10-25" categories: [Actuarial Science, AI Agents, VM-22, Python] image: thumbnail.png jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false warning: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Note.** This is a personal, educational project built on synthetic data. It is not a compliant VM-22 valuation, and the views here are my own, not my employer's. The code is on GitHub: [Ouo15/vm22-agent](https://github.com/Ouo15/vm22-agent). ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Try it yourself:** [vm22-agent.streamlit.app](https://vm22-agent.streamlit.app/). The Results tab runs valuations, the SERT and sensitivities with no setup. To chat with the agent, paste your own Anthropic API key. It stays in your browser session's memory and is never stored. ::: VM-22, the NAIC's principle-based reserving (PBR) framework for non-variable annuities, applies to new business from 2026, with a three-year transition before it becomes mandatory in 2029 ([Milliman](https://www.milliman.com/en/insight/vm-22-readiness-key-consideration)). For fixed and payout annuity writers, that means stochastic exclusion tests, deterministic and stochastic reserves, prudent-estimate assumptions with margins, and a full VM-31 report documenting all of it. Much of that work is orchestration and documentation around a calculation engine, which is exactly where agentic AI can help. So I built one: a **VM-22 valuation agent** that runs the valuation, answers regulatory questions from the Valuation Manual's text, checks inputs and assumptions, and drafts both the technical report and a summary for executives. This post covers the design choices that matter most when you put a language model anywhere near a reserve number. ## The design principle: the model never computes a reserve A language model can explain a CTE, but it shouldn't calculate one. Actuarial numbers need to be exact, reproducible and auditable, so the project has two clearly separated layers: - A **deterministic actuarial engine** in Python, covered by unit tests, which does every calculation. - An **agent** (Claude, via the Anthropic API) that decides which calculations to run, interprets the results, grounds regulatory statements in the manual, and writes. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR U[Actuary] --> A[Streamlit app] A --> G[Agent: Claude] G -->|tool calls| T[10 tools] T --> E[Actuarial engine
SERT · DR · SR · floor · sensitivities] T --> V[Valuation Manual search
chapter + page citations] T --> C[Data and assumption checks] T --> R[Report drafts
VM-31 · stakeholder summary] E --> T ``` The agent works only through tools. Each one wraps a tested function and returns structured results: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `validate_inputs`, `review_assumptions` | Data checks; margins, bounds and unverified parameters | | `run_sert` | Stochastic Exclusion Ratio Test by reserving category | | `run_valuation` | Deterministic Reserve, Stochastic Reserve (CTE), floor, reported reserve | | `run_sensitivity` | One-assumption shocks: mortality, lapse, rates, spreads, expenses | | `search_valuation_manual` | Passages from the NAIC Valuation Manual with chapter and page | | `confirm_regulatory_parameter` | Marks a parameter as verified, only with a citation | | `save_report` | Saves the VM-31 draft or the stakeholder summary | ## The engine The engine values a synthetic block of **1,000 single-premium deferred fixed annuities** (7-year surrender charge, guaranteed minimum rates, dynamic lapses) and **400 payout annuities** (life-contingent, some with a certain period). For each economic scenario, it projects annual liability cash flows $CF_t$ and discounts them at the scenario's net earned rate. The **scenario reserve** is the starting asset amount needed so that the portfolio never runs out, which is the greatest cumulative present value of the cash flows: $$ \text{Reserve}_s = \max_{t} \sum_{k=1}^{t} CF_{s,k} \prod_{j=1}^{k} \frac{1}{1 + i_{s,j}} $$ From there: - The **Deterministic Reserve (DR)** is the scenario reserve on the baseline rate path. - The **Stochastic Reserve (SR)** is the conditional tail expectation of scenario reserves over 1,000 stochastic paths: the average of the worst 30% at CTE 70. - The **SERT** compares reserves under eight rate-stress scenarios with the baseline. A category that fails needs the Stochastic Reserve. - The **reported reserve** is the modeled reserve, subject to a cash-surrender-value floor for deferred annuities. A full 1,000-scenario valuation runs in about 1.3 seconds, which matters when an agent may call it several times in one conversation. ## What the synthetic block shows ::: {#a373941a .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=3} | Category | SERT ratio | Worst stress | DR | SR (CTE 70) | Floor | Reported | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Deferred | 3.6% | up shock 200 | $95.1M | $97.3M | $105.9M | **$105.9M** | | Payout | 7.8% | down shock 200 | $48.7M | $50.6M | – | **$50.6M** | | **Total** | | | $143.8M | $147.9M | $105.9M | **$156.4M** | ::: ::: Two results are worth a closer look, because they are the kind of findings the agent has to explain correctly: - **Deferred annuities: the floor binds.** The modeled reserve is below the cash surrender value, so the floor sets the reported reserve. The worst SERT stress is a *rise* in rates: competitors credit more, policyholders surrender, and assets must be sold to pay them. - **Payout annuities: the Stochastic Reserve applies.** They fail the exclusion test, and the worst stress is a *fall* in rates. There's no surrender option, so the risk is reinvesting at lower yields over a long payment stream. ::: {#cell-fig-distribution .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Payout annuities: distribution of scenario reserves over 1,000 stochastic interest-rate paths, with the Deterministic Reserve and the CTE 70 Stochastic Reserve.](index_files/figure-html/fig-distribution-output-1.png){#fig-distribution width=659 height=371} ::: ::: ## Guardrails that make the agent trustworthy The interesting part of an actuarial agent isn't the chat, it's the discipline around it. These are the rules I built in, both in code and in the agent's instructions. **1. Numbers only from tools.** Every reserve, ratio and sensitivity in a reply must come from a tool result in that conversation. If a figure isn't there, the agent says so and offers to run the tool, rather than estimating. **2. Regulatory claims are cited.** The NAIC Valuation Manual (loaded by the user as a PDF) is split into passages tagged with their chapter, such as VM-22 or VM-31, and page. The agent cites the passages it relies on. If the manual isn't loaded, or a search finds nothing, it has to say so. Background from the model's own knowledge must be labeled as unverified. **3. Unverified until proven.** This is the guardrail I like most. Every regulatory parameter (the CTE level, the SERT threshold, the number of scenarios, the floor basis) starts as **unverified** in a configuration file. The agent can mark one as verified only by calling a tool that *requires a citation* from the manual. Until then, the parameter is flagged in every result and report. In my experience, it's the parameters people assume they remember that end up wrong. **4. Validated tool inputs.** Every tool input is checked against its schema before the tool runs, and failures go back to the model as errors it can correct. **5. Tests on the actuarial core.** The engine's tests compare results with closed-form answers. For example, with mortality switched off, a payout annuity's reserve must equal an annuity-certain. The tests caught one real bug: the CTE averaged the worst **31** of 100 scenarios instead of 30, because `100 * (1 - 0.70)` is `30.000000000000004` in floating-point arithmetic. It's exactly the kind of error that an LLM checking its own arithmetic would never notice. ## Two reports, two audiences The same results feed two very different documents, and the agent drafts both: - A **VM-31-style technical draft** for the appointed actuary and regulators: data and validation, assumptions and margins, methodology, results by reserving category, sensitivities, and the limitations that need verification. - A **stakeholder summary** for executives: the bottom line first, what drives the reserve, key risks in plain words, and the decisions needed. Both are labeled drafts for review by a qualified actuary, and both export to Word. ## What it isn't, and what's next This is a learning project, and its simplifications are deliberate: - **Data:** the in-force block is synthetic. - **Economic scenarios:** a one-factor interest-rate model stands in for the NAIC's prescribed Generator of Economic Scenarios. - **Mortality:** a synthetic table stands in for the prescribed tables. - **Methodology:** the asset modeling and the reserve methodology are simplified. Natural next steps would be the prescribed scenario files and mortality tables, more products such as fixed indexed annuities, and an evaluation set of regulatory questions with known answers to measure how accurately the agent cites. The broader lesson applies well beyond VM-22. **In actuarial work, the value of an AI agent comes from what it is *not* allowed to do**: compute numbers itself, cite text it hasn't retrieved, or treat a parameter as settled without evidence. Within those limits, it takes on the orchestration and documentation work that consumes so much of a valuation cycle. You can try the **[live demo](https://vm22-agent.streamlit.app/)**, and the full code (MIT licensed), tests and setup instructions are on GitHub: **[github.com/Ouo15/vm22-agent](https://github.com/Ouo15/vm22-agent)**.
